items.title: Can HealthCare.gov force-change my plan variant mid-year due to an income increase?
items.body:
In January 2026, I enrolled in a Healthcare.gov Marketplace plan with no deductible. I also was anticipating low income for 2026.

In September 2026, I experienced an unexpected income increase. To avoid receiving excess Advance Premium Tax Credit (APTC) that I’d have to repay later, I called HealthCare.gov to update my income (the website frequently errors out, so the only way was to call). During the call, I explicitly asked the agent to keep me on my current plan so my accumulated deductible and out-of-pocket maximum progress wouldn't reset.

Yesterday, I received a new insurance card:

  1. Plan Name: Changed from Baylor Scott & White Marketplace HMO QHP / Bsw Premier HMO-Qhp to Baylor Scott & White HMO/PPO/EPO/TRS/Covenant / Bsw Plus HMO.
  2. Coverage: Benefits are significantly worse across the board - higher out-of-pocket maximum and a deductible.
  3. ID Numbers: Member ID remains identical; the Group number is almost the same, with a few extra digits added.

I called Baylor Scott & White (BSW), and they stated HealthCare.gov had enrolled me in a different plan variant (the last two digits of the Plan ID changed) and advised me to call HealthCare.gov back to switch me back.

When I called HealthCare.gov, the representative claimed I am still in the "same plan", but that my variant/tier changed because my higher income made me ineligible for my original level.

The two questions I have:

  1. Does HealthCare.gov’s explanation make sense - can coverage/tiers be force changed mid-year by healthcare.gov like this, because my income increased?
  2. If yes, why would anyone report a mid-year income increase on HealthCare.gov? Wouldn't it be better to simply reconcile APTC difference on April 15th? Or at least through w4, so that plan stays the same?

items.title: Is there any downside to using tax-deferred account with the intent of terminating before maturity?
items.body:
Imagine someone subject to taxation by the federal republic of germany (unbeschränkt steuerpflichtig) and planning to invest over a 20-year horizon.

  1. On a typical account used for buying and holding low-risk investment fund shares that person will use money that is already (income) taxed, and owe capital gains tax (Kapitalertragssteuer) upon every realization of profits, some of which will need to be paid in advance (Vorabpauschale), thereby limiting compound interest.

  2. On an account with otherwise matching composition over time but held under a contract qualified under the the new § 1 section (1b) AltZertG (Altersvorsorgedepot-Vertrag) it appears as if that person has the option of deferring taxes, up to the age of 70: Until that age they could terminate the contract early (§ 93 Schädliche Verwendung) and pay taxes on the lump sum. Which could realistically secure a huge advantage from compound interest, and even retain interest accrued from bonuses that were returned on cancellation. That is not how these retirement-oriented contracts are meant to be used - one is expected to receive regular payouts starting at some age between typically 65 or 70 - yet I do not see what would deter people from using them for other investing, with intent to cancel early from the outset.

The latter option sounds too much like a bargain, at the expense of federal budget. Where is the catch?

Reading related posts on the US "traditional IRA" type of account that seems to have served as an ideological template for the new German scheme, one would expect the catch to be a substantial tax disadvantage upon cancelling early. However, I have found no such disadvantage in the (sparse) information available so far.

(At the time of writing the question nobody can know the answer from having tried. There may be relevant differences from the existing section (1) contracts, and no section (1b) contract can possibly exist yet; certification is set to begin no earlier than 2027-01-01.)

items.title: Allocation of mortgage interest deduction between joint homeowners
items.body:
Two US taxpayers, A and B, own a home together as joint tenants. They both live in the home, and it is their "main home" for tax purposes. A and B are not married to each other and never have been, and they each file their taxes as "single".

There is a mortgage on the home, in the name of A and B jointly, and they each meet the criteria to take the home mortgage interest deduction. They each pay half of the monthly mortgage payments. Must they divide the deduction equally, or may they divide it unequally if this is advantageous to them?

For example, suppose that in a given year, the mortgage payments totaled $40,000, of which $10,000 was principal and $30,000 was interest. A and B each paid $20,000.

By default, each of them would say they paid $5,000 in principal and $15,000 in interest, and each would take a $15,000 mortgage interest deduction. But could they instead say that the $20,000 paid by A was entirely interest, and that B paid the entire $10,000 in principal plus the remaining $10,000 in interest? That would result in A taking a $20,000 deduction, and B taking a $10,000 deduction. This might be advantageous if A is in a higher tax bracket, or if A itemizes and B does not.

Pub. 936 (linked above) has a section "More than one borrower":

More than one borrower. If you and at least one other person (other than your spouse if you file a joint return) were liable for and paid interest on a mortgage that was for your home, and the other person received a Form 1098 showing the interest that was paid during the year, attach a statement to your paper return explaining this. Show how much of the interest each of you paid, and give the name and address of the person who received the form. Deduct your share of the interest on Schedule A (Form 1040), line 8b, and print “See attached” next to the line.

But it does not specify how the shares are to be determined.

Married Filing Separately - Who Can Deduct Mortgage Interest is similar, but in that case the taxpayers are married filing separately, and the mortgage is in the name of only one of them.

References to official information would be ideal.

(Bonus question: is there a legal way for A to deduct the entire $30,000 despite only actually paying $20,000 out of pocket? For instance, suppose that B gifts $20,000 to A (ignoring any gift tax implications), and A then pays the entire mortgage for the year and claims the full deduction.)

items.title: Does this work for a qualified covered call?
items.body:
Imagine an investor has owned the XYZ company (not a real company) for a long time with a low cost basis. He then writes an out of the money qualified call option against it.

The stock continues to go up. He does not want to pay tax on the capital gain at this time. He could buy back the call at a loss but the loss would be a long term capital loss. He would like to generate a short term capital loss. As a result, he does the following. He buys additional shares of the XYZ stock and then sells them at a loss. That should generate a short term capital loss.

I was told that I am wrong. Here is a reason why I think I might be wrong. The sale of a covered call is still a straddle for tax purposes. As such, I am thinking (but I am not sure of that) at the time you sell the calls you have to identify which shares are part of the covered call. As a result, you can not later claim that the shares you sold were the ones you just bought.

However, I feel I am right because of section 1092(c) of the tax code. Section 1092(c) says that covered calls are normally given an exemption from section 1092. For details on section 1092 you can look here: Text of section 1092

You will observe that section 1092 says: Section 1092(c)(4) provides an exception to the general rule that a straddle exists if a taxpayer holds stock and writes a call option on that stock. Under section 1092(c)(4), the ownership of stock and the issuance of a call option meeting certain requirements result in a qualified covered call, which is exempted from the general straddle rules of section 1092.

Therefore, I feel I am right. Am I?

As I understand it, donations of shares are not Gift Aid donations, Gift Aid being a mechanism that only applies to cash donations.

Does it therefore follow that:

  • giving shares to charity does not reduce my ANI at all, and therefore...
  • that it does not give me any relief from Personal Allowance tapering, whereas donating cash might do so, and therefore...

items.title: Can schedule C with expenses, but $0 revenue, help to reduce other w2, 1099g or 1099int taxable income?
items.body:
Taxpayers sometimes face a choice: Should they file Schedule C this year or wait until next year when actual income starts to appear?

My understanding is that IRS is strict about requiring you to demonstrate a profit-seeking motive to avoid reclassifying your business as a hobby. Showing income is obviously the litmus test that this is not hobby. However, the IRS is also understanding and recognizes that businesses in their first year may not generate any income (or even revenue) at all. For example, in app development, you might release a free version on the App Store and start monetizing only next year. However, you still had business related expenses like home office, Apple developer program subscription, startup costs etc.

My question: What are the key considerations for deciding tax year when to file your first Schedule C? In particular:

  1. Can expenses (home office, startup costs etc) on Schedule C (with no business revenue yet) reduce taxable income from other sources like W-2 wages, 1099-G (unemployment), or 1099-INT (interest) in the same tax year? If yes, how? I experimented in TurboTax, but home office expenses and startup costs didn't seem to affect my total taxable income that mostly came from w2 - am I missing something and entering those expenses incorrectly in TurboTax?
  2. If the answer to #1 is no, and the best you get from expenses is net loss carry-forward to next year, then why would the IRS ever be so keen trying to reclassify your business activity as a hobby? Especially if tax laws are designed in a way where you can't gain anything unless you start to sell your products or services?

items.body:

My employer is refusing to send a W-2 for 2024, saying that they have a 2023 W-2 and that is the correct one. However, my impression is that taxes should be paid the moment the money is made available to deposit, which it was not until mid-2024. It wasn't even close to 2023.

Which one of us is right in this situation? Should they issue me a W-2 for 2024? And if not, how can I proceed / will I be fined for non-payment of 2023 taxes? Thank you for the help.

EDIT: I read more on this, and the governing rule here seems to be 26 CFR § 1.451-2 Constructive receipt of income. It says that income is constructively received by the taxpayer for the year "during which it is credited to his account, set apart for him, or otherwise made available so that he may draw upon it at any time.".

However, the critical limitation follows: "income is not constructively received if the taxpayer's control of its receipt is subject to substantial limitations or restrictions."

The regulation provides a specific example in § 1.451-2(b) that's relevant to this situation: "if a dividend is declared payable on December 31 and the corporation followed its usual practice of paying the dividends by checks mailed so that the shareholders would not receive them until January of the following year, such dividends are not considered to have been constructively received in December." This means that the receipt of income is the moment of receipt of the check. The first check I received for this income was in the year 2024.

This seems contrary to the most upvoted answer. Can anyone help to reconcile these opposing views on the question? What is the a source supporting that the income was constructively received (and therefore taxes should be paid) in 2023?

items.title: Is my broker fee that was applied as mortgage points tax deductible?
items.body:

When obtaining my loan I opted not to purchase any points to lower my interest rate however my lender applied their broker fee as points to lower my rate for me which they made a big deal of by saying how generous they were being.

On my closing document for the mortgage under Loan costs I have the following table:

A. Origination Charges Borrower Paid
01. % of Loan Amount (Points) -
02. Application Fee $1,000.00
03. Broker Fee to my-mortgage-company $10,000.00

As well as tables B. Services Borrower Did Not Shop For and C. Services Borrower Did Shop For containing line items for things like: Appraisel Fee, Title Fees, etc.

However in the 1098 form provided to me by my mortgage company Box 6 contains the following: 6. Points paid on purchase of principal residence: $10,000.00

The verbiage in the IRS documentation makes me believe that this amount is not tax deductible:

  1. The points were computed as a percentage of the principal amount of the mortgage, and
  2. The amount shows clearly as points on your settlement statement.

As well as this item under Nondeductible costs to obtain a mortgage:

  1. Additional points the lender charges in lieu of other costs such as appraisal fees, inspection fees, title fees, attorney fees, and property taxes.

I'm leaning towards playing it safe and not adding this amount to my tax return but wanted to ask here to see if anyone had any other insights on this topic.

items.title: Is it generally wise to max out Health Care FSA enrollment when it is an option?
items.body:
My employer offers 3 health care plans and the cheapest one is a basic PPO plan. It has a pretty high deductible ($1.5k in-network single, twice that for family, double both for out-of-network) and combined out-of-pocket maximum ($9,450 single, $18,200 family). The medical OOP max is same as deductibles.

I took the basic PPO plan because I am relatively healthy. My spouse is too. But we are getting older and see doctors or specialists more than we used to. We also had our first child recently, which comes with numerous and uncertain expenses. Daycare for example is costly but enables us to bring home two salaries, and so it seems clear we should max out our Dependent Care Savings Account to spend on daycare.

What I'm trying to understand is my healthcare FSA contribution. Maximum I can contribute is $3.3k and I can rollover $300 into the next year. I figured, since this is pre-tax money, how much am I already paying in taxes anyway? My understanding - maybe this is where I need to be corrected - is that money into my FSA is taken out of money that would've gone to federal income tax withholding anyway. Well, from January to October I already had over $8k go to federal tax withholding. In that case, why wouldn't I max out my FSA every time, even if I don't spend half of it? I get to rollover $300 next year, and my dollars go to potential healthcare spending instead of eaten up by federal income tax.

Am I understanding that correctly? Or if not, where is my calculation awry, and how should I think of FSA contribution vs. federal tax withholdings (if the two should be considered together at all)?
